To put it more bluntly, white people didn't take land from people who lived on it for generations, but we took land from people who had lived on it for like 20 years, after they had bluntly taken the land from other people who had lived on the land for like 20 years, and so on.

One last point I make in my pod with @APompliano, is that much land that whites now occupy in the US West has been occupied much longer at this point by whites than by the tribes they displaced... despite the narrative that tribes lived peaceably on these lands for 10s of generations. 

The point was that before Europeans arrived, America was not a Kumbaya land of peace, but rather a vicious world of tribal warfare over land. And that many of the tribes that the whites displaced had only been on that land for a few years. 

In other words, before whites, tribes like the Lakota and others, had been massacring and displacing various other tribes long before the whites arrived. 

Basically, this continent was a bloody battleground long before Columbus set sail on the ocean blue in 1492.

I agree. That's why I said no grudge. But that is the way the world works. People fight and take land. Has always been that way and likely always will be. I'd add that many if not most of the tribal land that is claimed to have been stolen, was "stolen" by other Indian tribes only decades before whites took it. In other words, when whites got here, a lot of land was controlled by tribes who had only recently gained control of it via warfare against other tribes.

Just to add a little context: I have a grandmother, now passed, from Tennessee who did extensive family research and showed that while she and I are not direct descendants of David Crockett, we are of his sister, and thus of his grandparents. 

In 1777, there was a well-documented attack on the Crockett family, my ancestors, that resulted in my Great....(don't know how many greats) grandmother, Elizabeth Crockett, being killed by Dragging Canoe, a Cherokee war leader. 

I hold nothing against the Cherokee... this is obviously ancient history. I only brought it up in the pod to make a point that the frontier was a tough and brutal time... a time that was not dominated by white men killing every Indian in sight and taking their land, but rather a long, drawn-out, multi-decade war... a vicious and brutal war to be sure, but a war that ultimately had a winner. And on both sides, the impulse to kill brutally existed, and my ancestors suffered the consequences.

I think there's a lot of political mumbo-jumbo out there now pandering to a relatively small voting class, the younger generations under 40.

But in the end, the median age in the US is 38. 

That means that 50% of the entire population is roughly 38 or over. The other 50% is under, but only half of that can vote.

In other words, the voting electorate is absolutely dominated by those 38 or over. 

We vote, we are relatively wealthy, and we own the assets. 

What we are concerned about is not "affordability," but the continued increase in asset prices. 

We are willing to help out the younger folks, but only so long as it does not jeopardize asset prices.

That is reality.

At the end of the day, there is sooo much bs sentiment out there about affordability. It is all political bs.

Most adult Americans, who are by the numbers in the GenX/Boomer cohort, want inflation, asset price increases, and the status quo. 

But that sounds bad, so you never hear a politician or even a voter annunciate it, but deep down, that's what the majority of the voting populace wants.
At the end of the day, everyone, at least in a metaphorical sense, wants and needs to kill their father.
And at that point, there will be younger generations still, who want to destroy what you, currently younger generations have created. And the cycle goes on. Oedipus.

At some point, we will die, and then you will out number us. Then you will be able to put in policies that benefit you.

But until then, over our dead bodies, do you get to destroy what we created. 

Until then, deal with it.

I do not want "affordability." 

I want asset price inflation, especially for housing and stocks. 

I am not worried at all about the fact that some 29 year olds are finding it hard to afford to a house.

The current median age in the US is 39. Most US adults are boomers and gen xers.

We want what Gen zs don't want. so the battle goes on.

This is going to sound crazy, but it is absolutely true.

My father was raised by a man born in 1890. My biological grandfather died during WWII.

In 1943, when my father was 4, my grandmother, born in 1911, was left broke, widowed, with two kids and no money. But she was good looking.

At first, she had to put my Dad and aunt in an orphanage. Then she found a dude 20 years older, born around 1890, with some money, to marry. 

That man raised my Dad, and my Dad raised me. A man who never knew his father and had a strict upbringing by a man born a mere 25 years after the end of slavery.

I have always been raised not to expect shit from the government or other people.

If younger generations expect the older generations to somehow sacrifice their wealth, gained over decades, to make things easier on them, they are delusional. 

Boomers, and now to some extent Gen Xers, are getting comfortable in their lives and wealth position. 

The fact that homes are now expensive, AI is coming, and interest rates are high are for you younger folks to deal with.

Don't expect pity or help from us. Indeed, expect us to defend our advantageous positions against your interests. 

It's a jungle out there.
Honestly, from my experience, I think most US men in their 20s, 30s and 40s are a bunch of pussies who listen too much to their women and care too much about their skin.

In many if not most economic respects, Gen Z especially and to some extent Millennials, have it harder than Gen X and Boomers, not much harder, but a bit harder. 

So man up and deal with it. I'm so sick of hearing about the K-shaped economy... cry me a river. 

100 or so years ago, many people left their family, friends, culture, etc. to create a better life for their children and grandchildren. They succeeded on that front. 

But in some sense, their great-grandchildren need to forge ahead on their own.

The US was 50%+ of global GDP after WWII. We are not going back there.

The easy, good times for white, US-born men are over. 

So now it's time to man up. 

Deal with it and figure it out. I'm so sick of hearing sob stories from 30 year olds about "affordability."

All Americans in their 30s in the US now have the greatest opportunity set in front of them of any other population around the world.

The US is only 4% of the world population... but we're still like 20% of global GDP, not like the 50s, but still very advantageous. 

You have it all at your fingertips. Go work for it and figure it out. 

Stop your whining, effeminate complaining and make something of yourselves... and stop talking about "affordability."

Gen Zers and young Millennials bitching about housing need to grow a pair and do something about it. 

I'm a gen Xer with a 2.5% mortgage on a house I paid peanuts for over 15 years ago. I'm in the majority of American middle- to upper-class households who have absolutely no problem with housing.

What 20-30s folks need to recognize is that they are a minority of American adults. Most of us adults are very happy with our homes, the price we paid, and our mortgage rate. 

And guess what, men coming of age in the '40s got drafted and had to go fight for 4 years in Europe/Japan... and maybe die.

Men in the late '60s/'70s, same thing, but for Vietnam.

Now you have a challenge... housing is much less affordable than it used to be. Would you rather be drafted into WWII/Vietnam? 

I know that I wasn't, but I had my own challenges at my time. But that's not the point. The point is, have some pride and dignity.

Say, fuck boomers, fuck you guys, we're going to craft our own way... and then go do it.

Here's a  potential avenue... I think drones and vertical takeoff vehicles could open up land for homes everywhere. No roads needed. There are solutions. Let's find them. Not bitch about everything.

I'm afraid we are feeding/creating a generation (or two) of complainers, whiners, and brats. 

Life is not easy. 

From Buddha to Christ to the Old Testament, life is hard.  Human nature is flawed. You give people a bunch of free stuff, they take advantage, not take a hand up. 

To put it more simply, "It's a jungle out there."

My wife says I suffer from early onset of Grumpy Old Man syndrome, at 50 years old, maybe I do.

But look, I'm sorry if you were told your masters degree in Russian literature from Brown would produce a nice life and now it's not. 

You were fed a bunch of BS lies about education, etc. The reality is, society rewards tangible efforts to increase standards of living.

The WSJ just ran an article about electricians making over 1/4 million a year, riding around data center job sites in golf carts & supervising employees... with huge bonuses to boot. The guy they focused on in the article says, "he pinches himself everyday."

This is still the land of opportunity despite some mean reversion going on. 

The US was 50% of world GDP in the 50s and still we had a hugely bifurcated economy. Racial segregation was rampant. Women were not even considered for consequential roles. 

The US is still the best place to be with the most opportunity, but as always, simply playing it safe won't cut it.

I have to admit. I don't like telling people if they make under $140/year they are poor. It's all a money issue and with some policy changes we can change your life.

I think that a very select group of Americans, namely white, male, native-born heterosexual Christians had basically everything handed to them post WWII. 

You could literally fit into that class of people, be an idiot who barely graduated from HS, and go work 40-hours/week at a factory somewhere and live a great life.

But that was an illusion. A moment in time for a select group. It is not how life generally works.

How life generally works going back hundreds of years is like a pyramid. This is perhaps why all ancient cultures built pyramids. 

There is a huge base of poverty that enables a level of wealth at the top. It has been the same for millenia. It has not changed. And it still exists.

The best place in the world to move from that base to the top tiers has been, is, and likely will continue to be the US.

But if we tell all our young people that you are screwed. That you are just boomer-victims. Then they will start to believe that and demand that which they are not entitled to.

Take a chance. Risk something. Start a business. Leave the safety and comfort of your $100K/year job to make something of yourselves. 

Don't just sit around saying that everything is stacked against you. That life sucks. Poor you.

I want to defend my privilege vigorously and unapologetically.

A Respectful Counterpoint to Professor Plum

We are living in the most abundant, egalitarian, and luxurious time of human history. However, many are misconstruing a slight dip in white, European-descendant, male-supremacy and -luxury as an overall decline in the U.S./civilization’s upward trend.

I strongly disagree with the premise that we are now worse off than in the 1950s insofar as poverty is concerned.

@profplum99 wrote a thoughtful and well-researched piece about the poverty line. As he notes, it was constructed in the 1960s. He notes that the real poverty line at this point in time should be well over $100K. 

Perhaps. 

However, I would note the following: During the 1950s the U.S. also had a very bifurcated, k-shaped economy despite the misconception that it was a time of abundance for all.

In reality, it was a time of segregation. Immense wealth and opportunity gaps existed both racially and regionally. Indeed, according to historical estimates by the U.S. Census Bureau and economist Gordon Fisher, about 22%–25% of Americans lived below what would later be defined as the poverty line during the late 1950s. This compares to an official poverty rate of 10.6% in the U.S. for 2024.

Prof Plum puts a relevant chart showing this decline in the "official" poverty rate into his piece (linked/copied below). 

But let me not argue that we are better off than the 1950s, but that we are mostly in the same area. 

I think I can make that point. 

And moreover, I think I could make the point that we are mostly in the same area as we were in the 1850s, the 1750s, and indeed the 1550s.

In other words, my counterpoint to Prof Plum is that we are basically where we have been for 100s of years. There really has not been much improvement one way or the other of the societal/caste pyramid.

The difference now is that for the first time ever, the U.S. pyramid is not dominated by white, male, native-born people. 

A fifth-generation American man can now walk down the streets of the Fremont neighborhood in Seattle and see a 26-year-old Chinese-immigrant woman on a visa making twice his annual salary as she leaves her Google or Meta offices.

Does that piss that white guy off? Hell yeah it does. But does that mean that our society is now falling into irreputable disrepair. I think not.

Indeed, I think we are on the verge of actually fulfilling the dream of Jefferson: that all men (women) were created equal. We are on the verge of shifting the historical pyramid of society that goes back centuries. 

But it is always darkest before the dawn.

Do not let the Doom & Gloomers get you down! Do not get mired in the negativity and pessimism of folks like Prof Plum and @adamtaggert.

We are on the verge of greatness. We are correcting past wrongs and paving a pathway towards abundance.

Technology, AI, humanoids, indeed all the blessings that God has provided for us are now finally starting to be harnessed. 

Energy, compute, intelligence, all is before us. Do not let some envious or puritanical-bent get you into the grey.

I’ll give an example. A week or two ago I actually listened to the entire conversation between Prof Plum and Adam Taggert on Thoughtful Money. 

It was all doom and gloom, very sad, and then, incredibly, the outlook of Prof Plum on equities is that their path is higher—but he was somehow disappointed by this because he thought it was driven by passive flows.

What’s more, Adam openly admitted that he been involved in tech back in the day, then left it, and has now seen people of mediocre ability become immensely richer than he because of GOOG or NVDA stock options and that he was jealous. 

In other words, the whole show was the two of them saying stocks are going higher, but we are sad (Greene) and jealous (Taggert) about it. 

What?? 

What the hell is that???

Look, I just watched the whole Ken Burns' “Revolution” series this past week. 

Here’s a reality check: The world has never been fair. There have always been and still currently is a huge percentage of the population living in poverty. 

Perhaps, in the ‘50s, if you just focused on white people in the U.S., it seemed like a utopian time had occurred. 

But go ask the black man, grandson of slaves in Durham, NC if the 1950s were a great time to live.

The global pyramid of supremacy is being rewritten. 

I just listened to an interview on Bloomberg last night with the CEO of FoxCom. He was asked about manufacturing in the U.S. and what the biggest challenge is. 

His response: shortage of workers, not of bodies, but of people who are willing and able to do the work demanded. 

That FoxCom CEO went on to say he knows he needs to work with local and federal governments to get the people trained up and ready to go.

This is going to happen. It will take time, but the overall trajectory of U.S. population standard of living is rising. One in five children used to never see their 5th birthday just a short time ago in the broad span of human history. 

The difference today is that some white folks with college degrees are no longer in the “favored” class. 

Blaming things on index investing or fiat currency is in my mind a cop out. We are working through huge inequalities that have existed in all human societies for centuries. 

It’s just now race/gender aren’t clear definers of economic potential. Overall levels of poverty are mostly in line with long-run historical averages, if not, they are lower and going lower every day. More people around the world are getting healthcare, eating protein, having dental care, etc. than ever before. 

Go back to the ‘50s. There were plenty of black/brown/recent immigrant neighborhoods just a mile or two from the Loop in Chicago to be found without running water, rampant diseases, and overall horror. 

This is the history of America. 

A wealthy country filled with struggling poor; however, now some entitled whites find themselves in the poverty mix. 

We can and will do better, but let us not delude ourselves into thinking we are now in some much worse place than we were 70 or 170 years ago. 

We are in a better place and getting better every day.

Lastly, as I mentioned, the 1950s had huge swaths of poverty and inequality. Eventually these disparities led to social upheaval and massive cultural changes during the 1960s, but they were able to coexist during a time of spectacular stock market performance. 

The S&P turned out an average annual total return of 20.45% over the course of the 1950s, much better performance than the 1920s or even the 1990s could produce. And there was no dot-com bust or Great Depression as the calendar turned to 1960.

Unfortunately, the world is full of a history of a multitude of poor struggling to survive while the wealthy live lives of luxury. 

For most of U.S. history, a strict racial and ethnic segregation protected certain classes. 

Those protections have deteriorated in recent decades, leading many in those historically-protected classes to see the U.S. as on a downward trend. 

However, in the aggregate, irrespective of race or ethnic-background, that is just not the case.

Let’s continue the upward trend, rather than decry a false decline.

Is the Federal Reserve Unconstitutional? 

Part of the current case heading to the Supreme Court regarding tariffs revolves around Congress’s ability to delegate a Constitutionally given power, namely the power “To lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises" as given in the first clause of Article I, Section 8.

However, in the fifth clause of that exact same Article and Section, it also gives Congress the power “to coin money” and “regulate the Value thereof.” Indeed, the Supreme Court has also previously interpreted Congress's power "to coin Money" as granting it the authority to regulate all aspects of the nation's currency, including paper money, during a series of cases from the late 1800s known as the Legal Tender Cases. 

So, if Congress cannot delegate its taxing authority, does that also mean it can’t delegate its monetary authority? And if so, is the Federal Reserve, by extension, unconstitutional as well? Something to consider as the tariffs case proceeds.

When Andrew Jackson vetoed the charter renewal bill for the nation's 2nd central bank. He not only argued against the bank, but against the legitimacy of the Supreme Court to decide Constitutional issues vis-a-vis the Executive acting in his legislative capacity.  

The Trump Administration definitely has nothing on Jackson when it comes to a belief in strong Executive powers. 

An excerpt from Jackson's Bank Veto Message of 1832 (more complete text linked below):

"The Congress, the Executive, and the Court must each for itself be guided by its own opinion of the Constitution. Each public officer who takes an oath to support the Constitution swears that he will support it as he understands it, and not as it is understood by others. It is as much the duty of the House of Representatives, of the Senate, and of the President to decide upon the constitutionality of any bill or resolution which may be presented to them for passage or approval as it is of the supreme judges when it may be brought before them for judicial decision. The opinion of the judges has no more authority over Congress than the opinion of Congress has over the judges, and on that point the President is independent of both. The authority of the Supreme Court must not, therefore, be permitted to control the Congress or the Executive when acting in their legislative capacities, but to have only such influence as the force of their reasoning may deserve."

They will pin their hopes to a cocktail of MMT & AI deflationary forces. 

Case in point: In 2008, interest expense as a % of GDP was 1.7%. In 2020, it was 1.6%, a slight decline. Yet debt to GDP increased from 64.2% to 132.8% over that same period.

In 2021, interest expense was down to 1.49% of GDP and then doubled to roughly 3% despite debt/GDP staying relatively flat around 120%.

Bonds seem to be capitulating today to a future MMT-Fed controlled by DJT appointees that will force short-end rates down for an extended period of time. 

The evidence is the break lower in 10yr yields. 

The talking heads like to talk about how the long-end isn't controlled by the Fed. Let me explain why I disagree.

Ultimately and historically, the Fed responds on the short-end with a reaction function correlated to NGDP. This leads the long-end to price based on long-run expectations of NGDP which are of course a combo of inflation and real-growth.

However, this is fundamentally a secondary and anecdotal reaction function that has historically been taken for granted b/c the supposition is that short-end rates will correspond to NGDP expectations.

HOWEVER, if you presume that front-end rates will not respond higher b/c of higher NGDP, then you must go back to the ultimate and primary pricing mechanism of longer-term rates, which is a discounted sum of short-term rates. 

Once the market believes that short-term rates will not respond as historically has been the case (according to NGDP), it must, ultimately and reluctantly, begin to revert to its primary pricing mechanism which is a sum of short-term rates.

Bond market beginning, but just barely, to believe today that short-term rates are going to stay lower for longer (regardless of NGDP) and are beginning to price in the longer-end accordingly. 

This is a flattening, not a steeping that has been all the rage to talk about lately. 

We are heading toward a flatter and lower curve.

Text from the Full Employment and Balanced Growth Act of 1978 is interesting at this point in time. It directs the Fed to seek both 3% unemployment and 3% inflation. It is the only time that I know of where Congress passed into law a specific inflation target.

Granted, it was just for the initial 5-year period after passing the law and it was later amended not to include a specific target. But nonetheless. It is interesting.

As most central bank watchers know, the current 2% target is not mandated by law and comes from actions that the New Zealand central bank did decades ago. 

The only inflation target Congress has ever given/alluded to is 3%, with a 3% unemployment target.

And, and this is key language quoted here, the "policies and programs for reducing the rate of inflation shall be designed so as not to impede achievement of the goals and timetables specified in clause (1) of this subsection for the reduction of unemployment."

In other words, Congress mandated the Fed to get unemployment down to 3% with 3% inflation. However, if those goals come in conflict, disregard inflation and focus on employment.

Says a lot, don't you think?

This last post reminded me of my vagabond poet days in the late 90s/early 2000s. If anyone is interested, here's a few poems I wrote back then. Surprised I still had them in an old email that I sent to myself long after I wrote them. 

I was a much "deeper" guy in my 20s, but found it to be an evolutionary advantage to disregard all the truly important philosophical questions of life and focus on what's for dinner. 😉

"Slumber"

Falling from glorious cliffs,
Tumbling headfirst to the
Rocky valley below,
I hit my head upon the
Way and woke from
An unearthly dream.
Oxygen rushes back,
Senses quicken,
Yet calm breath
Betrays my gratitude
For being alive.
Searching high up on
The pristine peaks
Of wild ecstasy,
I could not find
My elusive quarry.
Down below, in the
Cactus and rock covered valley,
I lay sprawled,
Sprawled in an
Overwhelming abundance
Of just that which
I was searching for.

3.2.3

"Desert"

Trembling fear shakes the body
& wakes the soul into tomorrow.
Yet endurance builds and
Though the road gets steeper
& the path gets harder
We climb.
We climb.
We climb into atmospheric
Heights of carnal bliss--
Unadulterated vice growing
Eagerly in a palm oasis.
Under the weeds and grass,
Worms burrow their way
Into the never-ending night
Of the cold, dry desert ground.
Passing under cacti & jackrabbits,
They make their way, silently,
Like limbless ghosts
Crawling into oblivion.
Dancing in the distress
Of unfulfilled dreams
And living nightmares.
We too struggle to pass the test
And fall 6 feet into eternity--away--
Away from the nagging gap
Between God and man.

6.26.3

"Complaints"

Carpets & rugs are all
To be seen as I
Walk over the
Madness & mayhem of
God’s sense of humor.
Stinking up the place,
Like gym socks &
Jock straps, we creep
And crawl our way
Though the labyrinth of life.
Looking for the cheese
At the end of the puzzle,
What we find instead is
A note from the manufacturer:
“Thanks for playing, but
Sorry, this piece is not
An instant winner,”
Not a ticket to paradise
First class but a
One-way Greyhound bus pass
to a town
Outside of Boise, called
Nowhere.

2.23.99

If you want to learns something about how Social Security is funded, read this:

Trump signed an EO today regarding social security. I think it is so funny and ridiculous how the media is using it as an opportunity to talk about the "trust fund" running out of money soon. There is no trust fund. It is a fund filled with Treasury debt. 

Treasury redeems that debt on an ongoing basis already and then issues new public debt to make up the shortfall between incoming funds and outgoing payments. The fund is already insolvent and has been since 2020 when it began being run down. It reached a peak of $2.9 Trillion in 2020. Since then, it has been declining and the US has been issuing new publicly-held debt to fund the shortfall.

Works like this: SS goes to Treasury and redeems special issue Treasury bonds to make payments. Treasury goes to public markets to fund that redemption. There will be no step-up in publicly-held funding necessary when the "trust fund" goes dry. The shortfall is already being funded by newly issued publicly-held debt. 

We already fund any and all shortfall between incoming SS funds and outgoing payments with the issuance of new publicly-held debt. What we do is an accounting trick where we cancel out inter-governmental debt and then issue new publicly-held debt to pay the short fall. 

In other words, nothing magical will happen in 2033 or whenever SS "runs out." New publicly-held Treasury issuance will not change. For every $1 billion in short fall, we will issue $1 billion in new publicly-held debt, just as we already do. 

But we not be able to X-out $1 billion in debt on the balance sheet and make that new public debt neutral insofar as total US debt outstanding. Hence it's all accounting. Outstanding debt will increase, but new public debt issuance will not change by 1 cent. 

What we do need to do is amend the laws to make SS payable by new Treasury debt. It's already happening indirectly, but not allowed directly by statute in a technical sense. 

Do you really think Congress won't vote to keep things going as they already are to save SS? It will just make the total Outstanding debt of the Treasury increase on the balance sheet, but will not change, as I've said, by one cent, the amount of publicly-held debt that Treasury is already issuing. 

No one on TV or in the media really understands this. And very people anywhere else understand it either.

Some things to consider about the upcoming nomination from Trump for Kugler's vacant seat. 

If DJT wants someone to be chair next year who is not currently on the board, he has to nominate him/her for this vacancy. The new chair must be chosen from the board. Thus, if he wants Warsh to be the next chair, he must nominate him for this vacancy or take the chance that Powell does not resign as governor after his term as chair ends in May. Note, his term as governor does not end until after Trump's term ends (1/31/28).

Also note, the Kugler term is the only Governor opening scheduled for Trump's term. Hence, this could be his only shot to put someone on the board if Powell should decide to stay on. 

As a bit of irony, if Powell stays on after his term as chair expires, he would have precedent for doing so. This happened once before, when Marriner Eccles was not reappointed as Chair in 1948 but remained as a Governor until 1951. 

This is ironic for two reasons. 1) Eccles is who the Fed HQ building under scrutiny now is named after; and 2) during the period that Eccles served, the Fed basically answered to Treasury and was not independent. It did what FDR wanted to support the war, including yield curve control. 

All above said, I think Powell will resign as governor in May. Why would he put himself through more of this? So it's likely Trump will put in someone he thinks a possible chair, but if he doesn't like what he sees, he will get a do-over next year, or be able to elevate Waller to chair. 

Lastly, Philip Jefferson, the current vice chair, is in a similar situation. Trump will get a chance to nominate a new vice chair in Sept. of 2027, but Jefferson may decide to stay on as his governor term does not end until 2036.

The US has gained an overall 139K unemployed people over the past year, but that number for native-born women has jumped by 252K. What is going on here?

In some ways, Table A-7 is the most important/telling Table from this month's jobs report. It shows a breakdown for four broad categories of workers: foreign-born men/women & native-born men/women. 

The unemployment rate for foreign-born men is unchanged YoY at 3.8%. It has declined from 5.8% to 4.4% for foreign-born women over the last year. Were it not for this dramatic decline, the overall unemployment rate would be much higher. Indeed, it is clear that immigration policies are what's keeping the unemployment rate so low. Just look at what's happen to the native born.

Native-born men have seen a small rise in unemployment YoY, from 4.4 to 4.5%, but the real change is for native-born women: increasing from 4.5% to 4.8%, a full 0.6% higher than the overall rate of 4.2% and a 0.5% jump from the reported 4.3% unemployment rate just last month. 

In fact, the number of unemployed native-born women has increased from 2.973 million to 3.225 million, a jump of 252,000 over the past year. Over all groups, the number of unemployed has increased to 7.236 million vs. 7.097 million a year ago, or by 139,000. 

My take: Clearly immigration policy is skewing the unemployment lower by taking immigrants out of both the country as well as the tracking mechanisms. As for native-born women, my hunch is this has a lot to do with AI. 

Of all four groups, native-born women are the highest educated and most likely to be white-collar. We are seeing a much bigger/faster impact on the workforce by AI than the overall numbers suggest. If you have deeply studied MMT, this post isn't for you. It's for those who may think they understand it, but have not actually spent any time looking into it. 

Modern Monetary Theory, or some variant thereof, has taken hold in this administration. It has been a part of the left for some time. Hence, no matter who inhabits the White House in years to come, MMT-like theories will be driving policy for the foreseeable future. 

There are a number of academic papers and books available on the subject, but if you want a few podcasts to get you started, I post a few informative ones to start with below. 

MMT has historically been associated with the left, but it's not a political philosophy. According to L. Randall Wray, one of its founders, it's more of an apolitical framework for viewing how the modern monetary plumbing actually works. 

I certainly don't agree with all of it. And I definitely don't subscribe to a number of the the policy prescriptions that MMTers tend to support. But along with reading Murray N. Rothbard, Ludwig von Mises, and Adam Smith, I think it also makes sense to listen to what people like Randall Wray and Warren Mosler (@wbmosler) have to say. If you've never done so, maybe give one or two of these pods a listen.

In Defense of the Robinhood Investor/Trader

My thoughts on the condescending remarks by Jim Cramer this morning are in the post below, but here I’d like to briefly expand on why retail investors/traders are the new “smart” money.

-YouTube, AI, Substack, X, etc. have democratized financial knowledge and advice. Sure, everyone gets to have an opinion and some of it isn’t the best, but it’s out there for people to absorb, analyze, and factor into their decisions. 

-The @RobinhoodApp and others like it have brought trading costs down to almost zero and made available trading vehicles and strategies previously either cost prohibitive or inaccessible to retail.

-Given above, retail is finally able to capitalize on their natural advantages over institutional investors.

Let me explain. Even Warren Buffett will tell you that if he were only trading a few million-dollar book, he could kill the market. Size is his enemy. Retail can be quicker and more flexible, turn positions around on a dime for less than a dime. They are also not beholden to public calls made on TV that force people to hold onto viewpoints longer than they otherwise would. I could go on and on about this and the inherent weaknesses/conflicts embedded within traditional buy- and sell-side analysis, but that’s a whole other post maybe.

Anyway, that’s all I’ll say here about this, but I think today is an appropriate day to congratulate—or least acknowledge some respect for the Robinhood investor/trader—not demean them.

I point this out, because, while we have relatively moderate long-end rates now, there may come another time when their three mandates become very much in conflict as they were during Covid.

At such time, I think there will only be one way to get at least two of their mandates: QE in order to keep long-end rates moderate as well as maintain employment. Price stability may need to be sacrificed. In other words, sacrifice one to get two. I believe this is the tradeoff they made during Covid. 

If they focus only on price stability, they will likely lose maximum employment which in turn will lead to losing the long-end as people see massive job losses on the horizon and realize that deficits are about to go even more parabolic given anticipated lower tax receipts and higher transfer payments from said job losses.

Some Fed Basics: They do not have a dual mandate. They have many mandates including growing the money supply and ensuring that rates on the long-end stay moderate. 

Specifically, beyond bank supervision and creating the regional Fed banks, the primary purpose of the Fed per the Federal Reserve Act of 1913 is "to furnish an elastic currency [and] to afford means of rediscounting commercial paper."

Regarding the Board of Governors and the FOMC, Congress has given them this specific charge per 12 U.S. Code § 225a: "[They] shall maintain long run growth of the monetary and credit aggregates ... so as to promote effectively the goals of maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates."

I just wanted to point this out as a lot of the discussion you hear on X and elsewhere simply assumes the Fed has only two mandates, both of which have nothing to do with the long-end. That is false. Ensuring moderate rates on the long-end is just as much part of their mandate as are price stability and unemployment.

Here's just a sample of some of the back and forth going on back then. This is a memo from Treasury Secretary Connally to Nixon:

"The simple fact is that, given our present international economic and financial position, some monetary disturbances--which the press will label "crises"--are virtually inevitable. The test is whether these can be met without impairing our basic domestic (or international) objectives.

Far from "muddling through" the recent disturbance, I believe these essential objectives were maintained:

(1) Quite deliberately, we avoided a strong reaction. By maintaining, insofar as possible, the focus in Europe, we helped deflate concern over a "dollar crisis." Pressures for strong domestic action, either with respect to higher interest rates or strongly intensified controls (or both) never built up.

(2) International sentiment was calmed fairly quickly and effectively in the circumstances.

(3) By making the point that the "crisis" grew most immediately out of domestic German political and economic concerns, we helped limit the repercussions on the dollar and set the stage for maintaining the IMF's role in exercising surveillance over exchange rate practices. The latter seems to be Mr. McCracken's principal objective.

(4) Finally, and not least important, a basic spirit of cooperation has been maintained. Thus we retain a base for dealing promptly with two major problems:

(a) Achieving more influence over the Eurodollar market and short-term capital flows generally.

(b) Reaching a consensus on methods of attaining some needed flexibility in the exchange rate structure, without simply falling into the trap of "everyone for himself."

Changes in our present international economic and financial position must be achieved without--and this is the key--undermining confidence in the dollar and the general stability of the monetary system. Should we fail, forces of economic nationalism and isolation in one country after the other--including the United States--could become unmanageable.

I do not underestimate the extent to which the problems are complicated by differing views among economists and businessmen, and among countries. In particular, I believe we must realize there is a strong element of thinking within Europe that would take advantage of weakness or clumsiness on our part to promote the Common Market not as a partner but as a rival economic bloc, competing vigorously with the dollar and reducing or shutting out, as best it can, U.S. economic influence from a considerable portion of the world.

These threats to monetary and economic order will require action in a wide variety of areas. Most important is success in dealing with inflation and growth at home. In the vital areas of trade, aid, and a better sharing of defense costs, where a clear focus for Government policy-making has been absent, the Council on International Economic Policy obviously has a lead role.

But one distinction should be clear. As I have understood it, the genesis of CIEP did not lie in an idea it could or should take over the role of responsible operating agencies. In the international monetary area, that role, by law and tradition, lies under your direction with the Treasury, which, in turn, must operate in close coordination with the Federal Reserve.

Specifically, I fail to see the merit in convening CIEP to "reassert" in general terms a position with respect to exchange rate flexibility that only a few days ago I reiterated in Munich. In view of recent developments, it is hard for me to see how informed observers could think the flexibility issue is dead. But its specifics do involve difficult tactical as well as substantive questions upon which important countries are not agreed. These questions are under active review within the Treasury and in the Volcker Group.

Obviously, relevant CIEP agencies and Peter Peterson are being and will be kept informed--they are, indeed, participating. But I do not think it useful or productive to convene a CIEP meeting for the purpose of issuing a broad public statement reaffirming what everyone already knows but leaving unanswered all those difficult questions of substance and tactics that are the heart of the matter at present.

My understanding has been that you believe it is appropriate and desirable to continue to proceed in this area in the manner I have outlined. If this understanding is not correct, I assume you will so advise me.

John B. Connally"

The "Nixon Shock" of '71 whereby USD/gold convertibility was "temporarily" halted is so analogous to these times it's crazy. All the same concerns were there: deficit spending, trade imbalances, FX issues, tariffs, tax cuts, and more. 

Along with closing the gold window, Nixon also imposed a 10% across-the-board tariff, which he termed an "import surcharge." He proposed sweeping tax cuts but claimed they would be accompanied by a reduction in spending, which, as historical research has shown, he never really intended carrying through on. He also put in wage and price controls for good measure. 

There are key differences, however, with today. #1 of those in my book is oil. US was not the world's top producer back then as it is now. Instead, it was a massive oil importer, and that's what really messed up the 70s economically. So we'll see how this all unfolds. 

For those interested in this period, I would highly suggest reading Three Days at Camp David: How a Secret Meeting in 1971 Transformed the Global Economy by Jeffrey E. Garten published in 2021 by Harper.

Monthly Treasury Statement released this afternoon. Good tax receipts created a $258 billion surplus this April vs. $210 billion surplus last April. Of note is Total Borrowing from the Public decreased by $57 billion. Due to debt ceiling, gov't continues to fund itself out of the TGA. 

This will create a massive need for issuance once debt ceiling increased. 

For comparison, I looked at net new borrowing from the public last year. For the months Jan-April 2024, the gov't increased public debt by $541 billion.

Today's auto tariff clarifications and exemptions mark an important turning point in this whole tariff drama. To me, this is the first time I'm seeing something that could actually stick, makes sense (both politically and geopolitically), and, importantly, something companies will make long-term decisions based upon. 

First, auto plants are essential should a nation need to mobilize for war. They can be converted to all sorts of defense-related manufacturing purposes, as they were during WWII.

Second, they are important from a political perspective domestically. If these auto tariff arrangements (or something very close) holds into next year, as I suspect they will, it will be very hard for democratic politicians to advocate rolling them all back. Obviously it won't be up to them at that time, but they will be asked about it in the midterm campaigns. Same goes for 2028. In other words, they have legs, regardless of election outcomes in the coming years.

While they might not realize it today, in the coming months auto companies will come to accept this, and new plants will be forthcoming. Will be very hard for any democrat to try and fight against. 

In short, this is something that makes sense to me. It will drive US production, aligns with national defense goals, and is politically difficult to fight against. I do think it has inflationary aspects, but sustained, higher inflation is the only path I see forward for prevention of an economic collapse, so that's bullish from my perspective. Ultimately, with a relatively secure border, I believe wage gains can outpace overall inflation, a net positive for the average American with little in assets and much in debt.

Happy Easter everyone! Here’s some positive thoughts (though they may sound a little depressing at first) that were running through my head today as I enjoyed this beautiful Sunday in North Carolina.

The US is a bit like a retired former sports star. It had an amazing run for a while, roughly from WWII to the ‘90s, where it dominated and couldn’t be touched, despite being matched against a powerful foe.

But now the glitz and glamour are gone. We certainly can’t play like we used to, and we’ve blown all the money we made during our heyday. What’s worse, broken joints have us addicted to pain killers and opioids. In hopes of a lifeline, we’re reaching out to all the people we bailed out when we had money. The people who came to our parties and mooched off of us for years, but they’re not all as solid friends as we thought. In fact, some of them are even happy to see us off our prime.

So what’s our initial reaction: Let’s kick the drugs, get back in shape, and go for a comeback. Do what we’ve always done and regain our industrial and manufacturing supremacy. Not going to happen. Father Time is undefeated, and the league has a lot tougher competition than it used to.

What we need is a second act. Something new. Something that will make us even better than before, and that ain’t making millions of cheap flat screens. We need to play to our current strengths: tech, AI, innovation. Dominate the digital world the way we used to dominate the physical one. Yes, we need to rebuild some manufacturing and industrial capabilities to be sure, things necessary for defense and medical care, but let the rest of the world manufacture our bobbles. We need targeted incentives, subsidies, and tariffs to protect and grow critical areas, but we can’t cut off our noses to spite our faces.

But not everyone is born to code. What about the folks who don’t want to design apps? Well, fortunately we have two huge demands for labor staring at us in the face. And they can’t be outsourced to China. And you don’t need a master’s degree to compete. The first: We need to rebuild, expand, repair, and improve almost all our infrastructure, from roads to airports to bridges to public transit.  Second: We have a dire need for bodies to help take care of our aging population. You don’t need to be an MD or an RN to help people take a shit. Glamourous it is not, but if paid a fair wage, there are also other rewards to serving the elderly.

Ok, maybe, but this is like another Manhattan Project or Marshall Plan. How do we pay for all this? Who will want to buy our debt? How can we afford the interest payments? 

We can’t. So we don’t pay any, or at least not a market rate. Two of the greatest challenges this nation ever faced were the Civil War and WWII. And we sure as hell didn’t have the money to pay for it. But we did it anyway. How?

During the Civil War, Lincoln issued greenbacks via the Legal Tender Act of 1862. These United States notes were issued directly into circulation. No debt. No interest. Just printed. Inflationary, yes, but we returned to more sound money once the crisis passed.

We accomplished the same thing by different means to finance WWII: YCC or Yield Curve Control. The Fed just bought up whatever bonds the US needed to issue and capped the 10 yr at 2.5%. The short end stayed at 3/8, and we had a nice upward sloping curve. Again, inflationary, but that same inflation, when coupled with growth, ate away at the real value of all those bonds and eventually we got back to stable prices.

Now, none of this will be easy or quick, but trying to relive our glory days just won’t cut it. What we need is a multi-year inflationary boom where real wages go up, not down thanks to a flooding of labor supply. This inflationary boom will reset our debt to GDP to acceptable levels, and the growth will drive tax receipts and lay the foundation for a strong economy in the decades to come.

It also won’t be easy to convince the American people that inflation is a good thing, at least for a time. But there was a time and a party that advocated for similar policies in the aftermath of the Civil War. It was a populist party, hated by the wealthy and big banks, called the Greenback Labor Party. As Peter Cooper, one of their presidential candidates, stated at their 1876 convention:

"The paper currency, commonly called 'legal tenders' or 'greenbacks,' was actually paid out for value received as so much gold, when gold could not be obtained ... But whether our currency will always be on a par with gold or not, ... the commercial and industrial prosperity of a country do not depend upon the amount of gold and silver there is in circulation. Our prosperity must continually depend upon the industry, the enterprise, and the busy internal trade and a true independence of foreign nations, which a paper circulation ... has always been found to promote."

And here’s the final kicker. It’s not just us who needs this. Europe and Japan are basically in the same boat. China has it’s own issues, huge provincial and real estate-related debts loads, and the need to drive consumption. It could actually be a win for everyone. And unlike WWII, millions don’t have to die to achieve it. 

So there's my positive, almost resurrectionary, thoughts this Easter Sunday. Naïve and simple to be sure, but a man can dream can’t he?

Anyway, like I said, Happy Easter everybody.

If we're really heading into an economic/trade war, do we need war time monetary policy--or at least something like it? Here's a little history of how it worked during WWII per Grok:

During World War II, the Federal Reserve (Fed) implemented yield curve control (YCC) to support the U.S. government's war financing efforts by keeping borrowing costs low and stable. This was a critical period when the Treasury needed to issue massive amounts of debt to fund the war, and the Fed played a key role in ensuring that interest rates remained predictable and affordable. Here's how they did it:

Setting Interest Rate Caps: In 1942, the Fed and the Treasury reached an agreement to cap yields on government securities across the yield curve. 

Specifically: 

Short-term Treasury bills (3-month) were pegged at 0.375%.
Medium-term securities, like 1-year notes, were capped at around 0.875%.
Long-term bonds (e.g., 10-year and beyond) were held at a maximum yield of 2.5%.

These caps created a steep but controlled yield curve, ensuring low borrowing costs while still offering some return to investors.

Open Market Operations: To enforce these caps, the Fed actively intervened in the bond market. Whenever yields threatened to rise above the target levels—due to market pressures or insufficient demand—the Fed stepped in as a buyer of last resort. It purchased Treasury securities in large quantities using its balance sheet, effectively flooding the market with liquidity and pushing yields back down to the desired levels.

Unlimited Commitment: Unlike modern monetary policy, where the Fed might hint at flexibility, during WWII it made an explicit and unwavering commitment to buy whatever volume of bonds was necessary to maintain the caps. This was a "whatever it takes" approach, signaling to markets that resistance was futile—yields would stay at the pegged rates.

Coordination with the Treasury: The Fed effectively subordinated its independence to the Treasury’s needs during the war. The Treasury dictated the terms of debt issuance (e.g., maturities and volumes), and the Fed ensured those securities were absorbed at the agreed-upon yields. This blurred the lines between fiscal and monetary policy, as the Fed’s primary goal was to facilitate war financing rather than manage inflation or employment.

Mechanics in Practice: For example, if demand tapered off for long-term bonds and their yields crept toward 2.6% (above the 2.5% cap), the Fed would buy those bonds in the secondary market. This increased demand would drive prices up and yields back down, stabilizing the rate. The Fed’s balance sheet ballooned as a result, holding about $24 billion in government securities by 1947 (up from $2 billion pre-war).

This approach was a blunt but effective tool. It relied on the Fed’s ability to print money and its willingness to absorb unlimited debt, a stark contrast to today’s more nuanced monetary strategies. ? For Grok: What does it typically mean in emerging markets when the currency, the stock market and sovereign bond prices all move lower together? 

Answer: In emerging markets, when the currency, the stock market, and sovereign bond prices all move lower together, it typically signals a combination of economic distress, loss of investor confidence, and heightened risk perception. This phenomenon often reflects underlying vulnerabilities in the country's financial and economic system. Here’s a breakdown of what’s usually at play:

1. **Currency Depreciation**: A falling currency indicates that demand for the country’s money is weakening. This could stem from capital outflows (investors pulling money out), a trade imbalance (more imports than exports), or concerns about political or economic instability. It often raises the cost of imported goods and can fuel inflation, especially in import-reliant emerging markets.

2. **Stock Market Decline**: A drop in the stock market suggests investors are selling off equities, likely due to pessimism about the country’s economic growth prospects. This could be triggered by factors like slowing GDP growth, corporate earnings downgrades, or fears of policy missteps (e.g., excessive debt, fiscal deficits, or central bank mismanagement).

3. **Falling Sovereign Bond Prices**: Sovereign bonds losing value (which means yields are rising) indicate that investors see higher risk in lending to the government. This could reflect worries about the country’s ability to service its debt, especially if it’s denominated in foreign currencies (like USD) and the local currency is weakening. Higher yields signal a demand for greater compensation for that risk.

When these three move downward together, it’s often a symptom of a broader **crisis of confidence**. Investors may be reacting to a specific trigger—such as political turmoil, a sudden tightening of global financial conditions (e.g., U.S. interest rate hikes), a commodity price shock (for resource-dependent economies), or a banking sector collapse. This can create a vicious cycle: a weaker currency increases the burden of foreign-denominated debt, which spooks bond investors, while falling stock prices erode wealth and domestic confidence, prompting more capital flight.

Historically, this pattern has been seen in events like the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis or Turkey’s market turmoil in 2018, where external pressures and internal weaknesses amplified each other. It doesn’t always mean a full-blown crisis is imminent, but it’s a red flag that the market perceives significant risks ahead. Policymakers might need to step in with measures like interest rate hikes, capital controls, or IMF support to stabilize the situation—though such moves can have their own trade-offs.

@elonmusk The Social Security Trustees' report released in May 2024 (covering projections based on 2023 data) updated several assumptions compared to the May 2023 report (based on 2022 data). These changes reflect evolving economic, demographic, and program-specific trends, contributing to the combined OASDI Trust Fund depletion date shifting from 2034 to 2035. Here are the key assumption changes:

1. **Economic Growth and Productivity**: 
   - The 2024 report assumed stronger near-term economic performance. Real GDP growth was revised upward for 2023 and 2024, reflecting a robust recovery post-pandemic. The average annual real GDP growth rate over the 75-year projection period increased slightly from 2.3% in 2023 to 2.4% in 2024 under the intermediate assumptions.
   - Total factor productivity growth (a measure of efficiency in using labor and capital) was also raised slightly, from an average of 1.63% per year in the 2023 report to 1.66% in the 2024 report. This reflects optimism about technological and operational improvements.

2. **Labor Force Participation**:
   - Labor force participation rates were adjusted upward, particularly for older workers (ages 55-64), based on recent trends of people working longer. The 2024 report assumed a participation rate averaging 63.1% for this group by 2035, compared to 62.8% in the prior year’s projection. This boosts payroll tax revenue, a critical income source for the trust funds.

3. **Wage Growth**:
   - Real wage growth projections were improved slightly. The 2024 report assumed an average annual increase in real wages of 1.24% over the long term, up from 1.21% in 2023. Higher wages increase taxable payroll, strengthening the trust funds’ revenue base.

4. **Interest Rates**:
   - The ultimate real interest rate on trust fund assets (the rate after inflation) was raised from 2.3% in the 2023 report to 2.4% in the 2024 report. This reflects expectations of better returns on the Treasury securities held by the trust funds, slightly boosting their income.

5. **Inflation**:
   - Near-term inflation assumptions were adjusted downward for 2023 and 2024 compared to the prior report, reflecting a cooling Consumer Price Index (CPI-W). The ultimate inflation rate remained steady at 2.4% annually, but the lower short-term inflation reduced cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) slightly, easing immediate pressure on benefit payouts.

6. **Demographic Assumptions**:
   - Mortality rates were revised modestly. The 2024 report incorporated updated data showing slightly slower improvements in life expectancy than previously assumed, reducing the projected number of beneficiaries over time. The average life expectancy at age 65 was lowered by about 0.1 years compared to the 2023 report.
   - Birth rates (total fertility rate) remained stable at 1.9 children per woman in the long-term projection, unchanged from 2023, so this had no significant impact on the shift.

7. **Disability Incidence**:
   - Disability incidence rates were slightly lowered, reflecting a continued decline in new awards. The 2024 report assumed an ultimate age-sex-adjusted incidence rate of 4.8 per 1,000 insured workers, down from 4.9 in 2023. This strengthens the DI Trust Fund’s position specifically.

These updates collectively improved the trust funds’ financial outlook. The stronger economy, higher labor participation, and better wage growth increased projected revenue, while slower mortality improvements and lower disability incidence reduced some expenditure pressures. As a result, the combined OASDI depletion date moved from 2034 to 2035, and the OASI-only depletion date shifted from 2033 to 2034 (though the latter stabilized at 2033 in the final 2024 figures due to rounding and offsetting factors). The trustees emphasize these are still intermediate assumptions, and outcomes could vary under high-cost or low-cost scenarios, ranging from depletion as early as 2031 to never running out within the 75-year window.

In Book IV, Chapter 2 of The Wealth of Nations by Adam Smith, he lays out various cases and reasons that tariffs make sense, even for a free market capitalist. 

One is industries necessary for defense; another is when there is a tax on domestic production that foreigners don't pay. An argument could be made that USD status as reserve currency creates artificial strength in our currency that is a de facto tax on our labor which foreigners don't pay. However, even if one doubts that, Smith clearly argues for tariffs at least as high as those that are set upon one country by the other. 

Specifically, he states the following about retaliatory tariffs: "The case in which it may sometimes be a matter of deliberation how far it is proper to continue the free importation of certain foreign goods is, when some foreign nation restrains by high duties or prohibitions the importation of some of our manufactures into their country. Revenge in this case naturally dictates retaliation, and that we should impose the like duties and prohibitions upon the importation of some or all of their manufactures into ours. Nations, accordingly, seldom fail to retaliate in this manner."
